overview: Channel Infrastructure (formerly Refining NZ) owns and operates New Zealand's only fuel import terminal at Marsden Point, comprising deep-water jetties, ~290ML of active storage tanks, an Independent Petroleum Laboratory, and the country's only pipeline (170km) carrying liquid fuel to Auckland. Having closed its oil refinery in April 2022 and converted the site to an import-only terminal, the company now earns contracted, largely fixed and inflation-linked infrastructure income from three fuel majors (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) rather than volatile refining margins, and is pursuing a multi-decade redevelopment of its 180-hectare Marsden Point site (the 'Energy Precinct') alongside a first international step-out into Melbourne's jet fuel supply chain.

business_model.summary: Channel earns take-or-pay style infrastructure income under 10-year Terminal Services Agreements (from April 2022 to 2032) with bp, Mobil and Z Energy, covering 100% of its private storage and pipeline capacity. Revenue is a mix of fixed terminal fees, throughput/variable fees, and Contracted Storage Agreements (capacity-based fees for product storage and transmix handling, independent of throughput), plus a small fuel-testing laboratory business (IPL). Nearly all Terminal Services and Contracted Storage fees escalate annually with NZ PPI (one-year lag), giving embedded inflation protection. Revenue has structurally fallen from ~$359m (FY2018, refining era) to ~$140m (FY2025, terminal era) but EBITDA margin has risen sharply (67% in FY2025) because the business no longer bears refining feedstock/commodity risk -- it is now closer to a regulated-like infrastructure annuity than an industrial refiner.
business_model.customer_type: B2B, extremely concentrated -- three fuel majors (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) plus, from late 2025, the NZ Government (diesel strategic reserve contract) and from 2026, Higgins/Vinci (bitumen terminal tenant)
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand (~100% of legacy revenue, one reportable segment); first international exposure from November 2025 via a 25% interest in the Somerton jet fuel pipeline serving Melbourne Airport, Australia

main_competitors: No direct domestic competitor for pipeline-delivered Auckland fuel supply
Alternative coastal import terminals/berths (smaller scale, no pipeline to Auckland)
Road/rail fuel logistics as a partial substitute for smaller volumes
Long-term substitute: EV/aviation decarbonisation reducing liquid fuel demand
competitive_position.market_position: Sole owner of New Zealand's only pipeline capable of transporting liquid fuel to Auckland; supplies ~40% of NZ's total liquid transport fuel demand and ~80% of NZ's jet fuel (including virtually all of Auckland International Airport's jet fuel). Effectively a natural monopoly infrastructure asset for the upper North Island.

moat_factors.description: Only deep-water harbour/jetty and only pipeline able to move liquid fuel to Auckland; replicating this would require immense capital, consenting and land access that competitors do not have

10-year Terminal Services Agreements with bp, Mobil and Z Energy (to 2032) covering 100% of private storage/pipeline capacity, with PPI-linked fee escalation, providing highly visible, low-volatility cash flow
Exxon Mobil (~14%), Ampol/bp-related holders are also among Channel's largest shareholders, aligning incentives around long-term infrastructure economics rather than adversarial renegotiation

Designated critical national infrastructure; central to NZ's Minimum Stockholding Obligation and now hosts the country's first Government strategic diesel reserve, giving Channel quasi-regulatory standing and government relationships

180 hectares of zoned industrial land (only ~1/3 utilised), with existing gas/water/electricity grid connections, offering multiple option value pathways (biorefinery/SAF, hydrogen, diesel peaker, additional storage) without requiring greenfield permitting

weaknesses: Extreme customer concentration -- three counterparties (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) represent the substantial majority of contracted revenue; any credit or relationship deterioration is material
Structurally declining underlying volumes long-term as light vehicle EV penetration erodes petrol/diesel throughput (partially offset by fixed/take-or-pay fee structure)
Single-site concentration risk -- all core infrastructure sits at one coastal location exposed to storms, seismic and other physical/climate risks

Growth optionality (biorefinery, diesel peaker, Special Planning Zone) is largely third-party/consortium- and government-policy-dependent, with long lead times and uncertain final investment decisions

Government/taxpayer deals (e.g., diesel reserve contract) attract political and media scrutiny over sole-source pricing, which is a reputational/regulatory risk even though currently revenue-accretive

growth_drivers: Marsden Point Energy Precinct redevelopment -- PwC estimates the projects under contemplation could add ~$3.3bn to NZ GDP and ~20,000 construction jobs, and ~$290m annual GDP plus ~1,150 FTE jobs once operational; $30m committed in 2025 for enabling infrastructure (new control room/admin building) ahead of precinct build-out

Marsden Point Biorefinery consortium (Seadra Energy, with Qantas, Air New Zealand, Renova, Kent, ANZ Bank, Ballance Agri-Nutrients) targeting >$1bn private investment and up to 400 million litres/year of SAF, biodiesel, urea and fertiliser production; final investment decision expected in 2026

New contracted storage growth -- four contracts signed over 2024-2025 delivering ~$170m of incremental revenue over 15 years (pre-PPI indexation), including the Z Energy jet fuel storage tank (now tracking ~6 months ahead of schedule, expected Q3 2026) and the Higgins/Vinci bitumen import terminal (contract value increased to ~$57m over 15 years, commencing Q4 2026)

NZ Government strategic diesel reserve -- $21.6m Regional Infrastructure Fund-funded recommissioning of ~93 million litres of dormant tank capacity, generating ~$1.2m/month under contract to end-2027, opened July 2026, with potential for further government fuel-security-driven demand as the Minimum Stockholding Obligation tightens (diesel holdings to 28 days by July 2028)

International step-out -- 25% acquisition of the Somerton jet fuel pipeline serving Melbourne Airport (A$14.1m, November 2025), expected cash-flow accretive from FY2026, with identified adjacent growth opportunities in the Melbourne jet fuel supply chain

Potential Special Planning Zone designation -- Channel remains under active consideration as one of NZ's first Special Planning Zones, a policy lever that could accelerate consenting for precinct development

Diesel-fired 72MW electricity peaking plant (FEED completed, funded by two electricity market participants) -- paused pending Government LNG import facility decision, but retains optionality given existing fuel storage and site infrastructure
Dividend Reinvestment Plan (21% uptake at FY25 final dividend) supporting balance sheet flexibility for growth funding

business.description: bp, Mobil and Z Energy account for the vast majority of contracted revenue; loss, distress, or aggressive renegotiation by any one materially impacts the business

EV penetration reduces petrol/diesel throughput over time; jet fuel is more resilient near-term (volumes at highest since 2019 in FY2025) but long-term aviation decarbonisation is a multi-decade risk, partly mitigated by fixed take-or-pay fee components and 'drop-in' biofuel compatibility

Biorefinery, diesel peaker and other precinct projects depend on third-party consortium decisions, government policy (e.g., paused pending LNG facility review) and lengthy consenting; final investment decisions can slip
All critical assets (jetties, pipeline, tanks) concentrated at one coastal Northland site exposed to storms, seismic events and process safety incidents

financial.description: Net debt $330m at FY2025 (3.6x EBITDA), within newly broadened BBB/BBB+ shadow credit target of 3.0x-4.5x; debt-funded acquisitions (e.g., Somerton) and growth capex increase leverage headroom usage

Retained earnings are deeply negative (-$293m at H1 2026) offset by a $726m revaluation reserve from the FY2024 asset revaluation; equity quality is sensitive to future independent asset revaluations (reviewed at least every 3 years)
Somerton pipeline stake introduces AUD-denominated earnings and NZD/AUD translation risk as Australian step-out grows

regulatory.description: Government mandates on fuel storage (28 days diesel by July 2028) are a growth driver today, but policy could shift (e.g., government choosing to own rather than rent storage, or alternative suppliers) reducing future government-linked revenue
Media/political criticism (e.g., NZ Herald) of the $21.6m diesel reserve deal as a non-competitive, politically-brokered arrangement creates reputational and potential future-tender risk

$79.3m of provisions relate to legacy refinery shutdown, decommissioning and site restoration, including an ongoing legacy hydrocarbon plume in the Northern tank farm requiring monitoring and remediation
December 2025 ASX foreign-exempt listing adds incremental compliance and one-off costs (~$1m in FY2025) alongside NZX/FMA oversight

macro.risk: Global fuel/energy price and shipping shocks
macro.description: Fixed-fee-dominant model insulates Channel directly, but severe/prolonged global disruption (e.g., Middle East tensions cited in 2026) could affect customer throughput or, conversely, boost storage demand as seen in 2026
$330m net debt at 5.1% effective rate; refinancing risk and higher-for-longer rates increase financing costs, though weighted average debt maturity is 3.6 years with no near-term maturities
Fixed take-or-pay revenue components provide resilience to NZ economic cycles, though variable/throughput fee components have some correlation to economic activity and transport demand

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand liquid fuel demand (petrol/diesel) is expected to plateau/gradually decline over the long term as EV penetration rises, per the Envisory forecast commissioned by Channel in 2024, though petrol demand has been running ahead of that forecast. Jet fuel demand remains robust, near multi-year highs in FY2025. Government energy security policy (Minimum Stockholding Obligation, strategic reserves) is a structural tailwind for storage demand through at least 2028.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low to moderate -- majority of revenue is fixed/take-or-pay under long-term contracts with PPI escalation; variable/throughput fees provide modest cyclical sensitivity to fuel consumption and economic activity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- geared balance sheet (3.6x EBITDA net debt/EBITDA) with weighted average 3.6-year debt maturity; higher rates increase financing costs but effective rate (5.1%) reflects mostly fixed-rate debt
key_input_costs: No longer exposed to crude oil/refining margin risk since 2022 conversion

recent_developments.event: NZ Government opened its first strategic diesel reserve at Marsden Point (93 million litres, ~9 days of national diesel demand); Channel refurbished three dormant tanks in ~9 weeks and receives ~$1.2m/month under contract to end-2027

Channel raised FY2026 underlying profit/EBITDA guidance to $97-105m (from $95-100m), citing faster-than-expected government storage fill, the Z Energy jet tank running ~6 months ahead of schedule, and higher Higgins bitumen terminal contract value (revenue increased from ~$45m to ~$57m over the contract term)

Government committed up to $21.6m from the Regional Infrastructure Fund to Channel for additional diesel storage amid Middle East (Iran-related) fuel supply disruption concerns; deal drew media criticism (NZ Herald) over lack of competitive tender
MBIE confirmed NZ fuel stock levels 'healthy' amid global supply disruption concerns tied to Middle East tensions

FY2025 annual result: revenue $140.2m (+0.3% YoY), EBITDA $93.4m (vs $95.1m FY2024, pro-forma ex-Wiri lease EBITDA up from $89.1m to $92.4m), Normalised FCF $66.9m (72% conversion), net debt $330m (3.6x EBITDA), FY2026 EBITDA guidance issued at $95-100m, maintenance capex guidance 8-10% of revenue
Completed foreign exempt dual listing on the ASX (ticker CHI), broadening the institutional/retail shareholder base
Acquired 25% interest in the Somerton jet fuel pipeline to Melbourne Airport for A$14.1m (debt-funded) -- first international/Australian step-out, expected cash-flow accretive from FY2026
'Sod-turning' ceremony with Minister for Infrastructure Chris Bishop for the new Higgins (soon Vinci Group) bitumen import terminal, construction commencing Q4 2026

Extension to additional storage contract secured, generating ~$50m of additional revenue over a nine-year extension term (pre-PPI indexation), commencing Q1 2028; capital allocation framework refreshed with dividend payout ratio increased to 70-90% of Normalised FCF (from 60-70%) and broadened target credit metrics to shadow BBB/BBB+ (3.0x-4.5x net debt/EBITDA)
Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRP) introduced at half-year results, achieving 21% uptake at the FY25 final dividend (1% discount to market price)
Legacy Wiri lease (1990s arrangement) expired, with legal ownership of Wiri terminal assets reverting to bp, Mobil and Z Energy

guidance.as_of: May 2026 trading update (updating Feb 2026 FY2025 result guidance)

items.notes: Raised in May 2026 from original $95-100m guidance given at the Feb 2026 FY2025 result, driven by faster government diesel storage fill, an accelerated Z Energy jet tank (Q3 2026 vs original Q1 2027), and higher Higgins bitumen contract economics
Consistent with FY2025 guidance; FY2025 actual maintenance capex was $12m

items.period: Ongoing (from May 2025 Capital Allocation Framework refresh)
items.notes: Increased from 60-70% previously, reflecting Board confidence in outlook and access to growth capital

Broadened from a shadow BBB+-only target to provide funding flexibility for growth; management does not expect a near-term step-change in leverage absent major new growth commitments; actual FY2025 leverage was 3.6x
25% Melbourne jet pipeline stake acquired November 2025 expected to contribute positively to FY2026 cash flow

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Rob Buchanan and the Board characterised the FY2026 guidance uplift as reflecting tailwinds 'embedded in near term earnings rather than one-off windfalls,' citing structural demand for fuel security storage. Management reiterated the Marsden Point Energy Precinct (biorefinery final investment decision expected 2026, $30m committed infrastructure upgrades) as the number one growth priority, while continuing to evaluate 'measured step-out' acquisitions in NZ and Australia within disciplined investment criteria, following the Somerton pipeline transaction.

bull_case: Effectively a natural-monopoly infrastructure asset (sole pipeline to Auckland, deep-water jetties) generating highly predictable, PPI-linked, take-or-pay contracted cash flows through 2032 with three investment-grade-quality fuel major counterparties

Multiple concurrent, largely capital-light growth vectors already converting to contracted revenue -- $170m+ of new contracts signed over two years, government diesel storage income, and international Australian expansion via Somerton -- with limited execution risk relative to the potential multi-billion-dollar Marsden Point Energy Precinct optionality

Guidance has been raised mid-year (FY2026 EBITDA to $97-105m from $95-100m) on structural, not one-off, drivers, evidencing positive earnings momentum and management credibility (four consecutive years of on-time, on-budget project delivery)

Rising, well-covered dividend (13.0 cps FY2025, up from 7.0 cps FY2022) with a now more generous 70-90% FCF payout policy and DRP option, appealing to income-focused NZX/ASX investors seeking a bond-like yield with growth upside

Government/regulatory tailwinds (Minimum Stockholding Obligation tightening to 2028, strategic diesel reserve, potential Special Planning Zone status) increasingly position Channel as a quasi-utility national-security asset rather than a discretionary energy company, potentially supporting a re-rating
bear_case: Extreme customer concentration (three fuel majors plus a headline-risk-prone government contract) means the investment case rests on continued goodwill and contract renewal from a handful of counterparties; consensus analyst rating is currently a 'Hold' with price targets (~NZ$2.6-3.0) clustered near or below the recent share price (~NZ$3.16, +53% over the past year) after a strong run

Long-term structural volume decline from EV adoption in light vehicles, and eventual (if slower) aviation decarbonisation, works against throughput-linked revenue even though fixed fees provide a buffer

The most transformational growth option -- the Marsden Point biorefinery/SAF project -- remains a third-party consortium decision (FID still pending in 2026) with large execution, financing and consenting risk, and other precinct projects (diesel peaker) are on hold pending government policy on LNG imports

Political/media scrutiny of sole-sourced, non-competitive government contracts (diesel reserve) creates reputational and future-tender risk, and could invite calls for the government to build/own rather than rent strategic storage

Balance sheet carries $330m of net debt (3.6x EBITDA) funding growth and acquisitions, and the FY2024 equity re-rating (to ~$818m/net assets) was substantially a non-cash asset revaluation rather than earned capital, meaning reported book value is sensitive to future independent valuation assumptions (fuel demand forecasts, discount rates)
